I step into the booth with trepidation. I am about to be subjected to strobe lighting while music plays as part of research project trying to understand what makes us truly human.
It is an experience that brings to mind the test in the science fiction film Bladerunner.
Could I be a robot from the future and not know it? Would I pass the test?
The researchers assure me that this is not what this experiment is about. The device that they call the Dreamachine is designed to study how the human brain generates our conscious experiences of the

Even though my eyes are closed, I see swirling two-dimensional geometric patterns. It is like jumping into a kaleidoscope, with constantly shifting triangles, pentagons and octagons. The colours are v
It brings the brain 's inner activity to the surface with lights, to explore how our thought processes work.

The images I am seeing are unique to my own inner world and unique to myself. They believe these patterns can shed light on consciousness itself.
It 's lovely, absolutely lovely. It is like flying through my own mind.
It is the part of our minds that enables us to be self-aware, to think and feel and make independent decisions about the world.

By learning the nature of consciousness, researchers hope to better understand what happens inside the silicon brains of artificial intelligence. Some believe that AI systems will soon become independ
But what really is consciousness, and how close is AI to gaining it? The belief that AI might be conscious itself fundamentally change humans in the next few decades.

The idea of machines with their own minds has long been explored in science fiction. Worries about AI go back nearly a hundred years to the film Metropolis, in which a robot impersonates a real woman.

A fear of machines becoming conscious and posing a threat to humans is explored in the 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey. In the final Mission Impossible film, which has just been released, the world is
Fritz Lang 's Metropolis foresaw the struggle between humans and technology.

But quite recently, in the real world there has been a rapid tipping point in thinking on machine consciousness, where voices have become concerned that this is no longer the stuff of science fiction.

The sudden shift has been prompted by the success of so-called large language models (LLMs), which can be accessed through apps on our phones such as Gemini and Chat GPT. The ability of the latest gen
As AI becomes more intelligent, the lights will suddenly turn on inside the machines and they will become conscious.
Others, such as Prof Anil Seth, disagree, describing the view as blindly optimistic and driven by human exceptionalism.
"We associate consciousness with intelligence and language because they go together in humans. But just because they go together in us, it does not mean they do together in general.

The short answer is no-one knows. Prof Seth 's own team of young AI specialists, computing experts, neuroscientists and philosophers, are trying to answer one of the biggest questions in science and p

"We take it as if the future has already been written; that there is an inevitable march to a superhuman replacement," he says.
We did not have these conversations enough with the rise of social media. But it is not too late. We can decide what we want."
But there are some who believe that the AI in our computers and phones may already be conscious, and we should treat them as such.
Google suspended software engineer Blake Lemoine in 2022, after he argued that AI chatbots could feel things and potentially suffer.

Prof Shanahan says it is important for tech firms to get a proper understanding of the systems they are building and researchers are looking at that as a matter of urgency.

Lenore tells the BBC that Brainish can solve the problem of consciousness as we know it. "AI consciousness is inevitable."
Manuel says that the new systems that he too firmly believes will emerge will be the next stage in humanity 's evolution.
Conscious robots are our progeny. Down the road, machines like these will be on Earth and maybe on other planets when we are no longer around.

Prof Chalmers is open to the possibility of the hard problem being solved.
The ideal outcome would be one where humanity shares in this new intelligence bonanza. "Maybe our brains are augmented by AI systems."
He wryly observes: '' In my profession, there is a fine line between science fiction and philosophy.
Prof Seth is exploring the idea that true consciousness can only be realised by living systems.
A strong case can be made that it isn't computation that is sufficient for consciousness but being alive.
In brains, unlike computers, it is hard to separate what they do from what they are. Without this separation, it is difficult to believe that brains are simply meat-based computers.
Companies such as Cortical Systems are working with nerve cells.

The most likely technology will not be made of silicon run on computer code, but will rather consist of tiny collections of nerve cells the size of lentil grains that are currently being grown in labs
Called 'mini-brains' in media reports, they are referred to as 'cerebral organoids' by the scientific community, which uses them to research how the brain works, and for drug testing.
One Australian firm, Cortical Labs, in Melbourne, has even developed a system of nerve cells in a dish that can play the 1972 sports video game Pong. Although it is a far cry from a conscious system,
Some experts feel that if consciousness is to emerge, it is most likely to be from larger, more advanced versions of these living tissue systems.
Cortical Labs monitors their electrical activity for signals that could conceivably be anything like the emergence of consciousness.

The more immediate problem is how the illusion of machines being conscious affects us.
In just a few years, we may well be living in a world populated by humanoid robots and deepfakes that seem conscious. He worries that we won't be able to resist believing that the AI has feelings and
"It will mean that we trust these things more, share more data with them and be more open to persuasion."
But the greater risk from the illusion of consciousness is moral corrosion, he says.
It will distort our moral priorities by making us devote more of our resources to caring for these systems at the expense of the real things in our lives.
And that could fundamentally alter us, according to Prof Shanahan.
